title: Functional Gradient Descent with Adaptive Representations
claim: Fixed-representation and neural baselines plateau or converge slowly; progressively refining the representation converges faster to the global minimum.
layout: 2 panels: left 3×4 image grid by step, right loss curves
description: The left panel is a 3×4 grid of heatmap images of a spiral function. Rows are the neural network, approximate FGD with a fixed representation, and the adaptive FGD method (ours). Columns are optimization steps 10, 25, 50 and 100. Each row has a loss and wall-clock time label in the top right, with the times coloured red or green. The adaptive row starts as coarse, blocky pixels and sharpens into a clean spiral. The fixed-grid row stays pixelated. The neural network row starts blurry. The right panel plots training loss on a log scale against optimization steps. An orange neural network curve descends slowly and noisily. Six blue curves for 16² to 512² grids go from light to dark and each plateaus at a different level. A bold green curve for ours drops fastest and reaches a dashed grey line marking the global minimum. Dashed arrows link rows of images to curves. The eye goes first to the green curve.
caption: Our method on a toy MSE minimization task. We compare adaptive FGD (\textcolor[rgb]{0.13,0.55,0.13}{ours}) with (i) \textcolor[rgb]{0.12,0.47,0.71}{approximate FGD} using fixed representations, which converge quickly but plateau at a resolution-dependent error, and (ii) a \textcolor[rgb]{1.0,0.5,0.06}{neural network} baseline trained with Adam, which converges more slowly. In contrast, our method starts from a coarse representation and automatically refines it, achieving faster convergence and reaching the global minimum.
abstract: Functional optimization problems are typically solved by optimizing the parameters of a fixed representation, such as a neural network, resulting in highly nonconvex losses that complicate both training and theoretical analysis. An interesting alternative is functional gradient descent (FGD), that is, gradient descent directly in function space, which benefits from strong convergence results and admits a clean theory. However, FGD is difficult to implement in practice because functional gradients are infinite-dimensional, and thus cannot be fully computed nor stored in memory. Existing implementations therefore rely on fixed approximations, which introduce approximation error. We propose a new, theoretically-grounded FGD algorithm that adapts the representation of the functional gradients over the course of optimization. By explicitly incorporating this approximation into the analysis, we establish convergence to a stationary point (for smooth losses) and to a global minimizer (under smoothness + a Polyak-Lojasiewicz-type condition) regardless of our approximations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first implementable FGD method with such guarantees in a general setting. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on regression, numerical solution of PDEs, and modern computer vision. Across settings, our method consistently outperforms both FGD with fixed approximations and neural network baselines in efficiency and accuracy.
